# Technical walkthrough — narration script and shot list

**Video:** `evidence/video/PhishGuard_Walkthrough.mp4` — 4:00, 1280×720, H.264, **silent**.
**Timeline of what is on screen:** `evidence/video/TIMING.md` (generated by the recording script).

> **This script is a draft for the student to record or replace.** It is written in
> the first person because that is how the narration must sound, but nobody has
> recorded it and no voice has been synthesised. Read it, change anything that
> does not match your own understanding, and record it in your own voice. If a
> sentence is something you could not defend in the live showcase, cut it.

## How to add narration

1. Open `PhishGuard_Walkthrough.mp4` in any editor that accepts an audio track
   (Clipchamp is built into Windows 11; DaVinci Resolve and Shotcut are free).
2. Record the narration below against the timings, then export as MP4/H.264.
3. Check the exported file plays with sound before submitting.

Alternatively, re-record the whole thing yourself with OBS Studio while speaking
live — the app is running, so nothing here needs Playwright. Use the shot list as
your route through the application.

## Segment 1 — 0:00–0:30 · Problem and final MVP

**On screen:** sign-in page, then a rejected sign-in showing the error banner.

> "This is PhishGuard, my MIT208 project. It addresses a gap in how organisations
> handle suspicious email: a filter that silently deletes messages destroys
> legitimate mail with no recourse, while one that only adds a warning leaves an
> untrained recipient to make a security decision. Neither records who decided
> what.
>
> PhishGuard holds suspicious mail instead of deleting it, shows an analyst
> exactly why each message was flagged, and gives the recipient a governed way to
> ask for it back. There are three roles — analyst, staff and admin.
>
> I'll sign in with a deliberately wrong password first, so you can see that the
> rejection comes from the API, not the browser."

---

## Segment 2 — 0:30–1:15 · Architecture and components

**On screen (0:30):** FastAPI `/docs`, scrolling through the endpoint groups.
**On screen (0:46):** `/system/database-status`, then `/health`.

> "The system has three parts. The frontend is React 18 with Vite, Tailwind and
> React Router. The backend is FastAPI with SQLAlchemy 2 and Pydantic v2. The
> database is PostgreSQL, with SQLite as a zero-install fallback for local work.
>
> This is the OpenAPI documentation FastAPI generates from my own route
> definitions — nineteen endpoints grouped into authentication, emails,
> release requests, audit logs and the dashboard. Each protected endpoint carries
> a bearer-token requirement.
>
> These two endpoints report live state rather than a hard-coded value.
> `database-status` tells me which engine is actually connected — and note it
> returns only the URL scheme, never credentials. `/health` runs a real query
> against the database, so `database_connected: true` means the connection was
> just tested, not assumed."

---

## Segment 3 — 1:15–2:20 · The main working user flow

**On screen (1:15):** analyst dashboard.
**On screen (1:25):** inbox, then the High Risk filter.
**On screen (1:35):** email detail with threat indicators, scrolling to the body.
**On screen (1:51):** staff portal, release request with an inadequate then a valid reason.

> "Signed in as an analyst, the dashboard aggregates the current state — how many
> messages are held, how many are confirmed phishing, the average risk score, and
> the spread across the last seven days. Every figure is scoped to the caller's
> role.
>
> The inbox is sorted by risk score, highest first. I'll filter to high risk only.
>
> This is the part I care about most. The score is a hundred out of a hundred, and
> underneath it are the specific reasons the rule engine produced that score: the
> display name claims PayPal but the domain is 'paypa1' with a numeral one;
> there's urgency language; it asks for a password; the link goes to a raw IP
> address; and the visible link text says paypal.com while the actual href points
> somewhere else. An analyst can judge each of those. That's why I used a
> transparent rule engine rather than a trained classifier — I can explain every
> point it awards.
>
> Now as a staff member. Notice this mailbox only contains mail addressed to this
> user — that filter is applied in the database query, not hidden in the
> interface. I want this message released, so I request it. A short reason is
> refused, because the analyst has to decide on this text alone. With a proper
> justification, it submits."

---

## Segment 4 — 2:20–3:10 · Packages, a decision, and a bug I fixed

**On screen (2:20):** clicking Request Email Release again → refusal.
**On screen (2:26):** analyst approves the request.
**On screen (2:42):** inbox showing the message released.

> "Here is one of the defects I found and fixed. Originally I could submit the
> same release request over and over — three identical requests all returned
> 201 Created, which filled the analyst queue with duplicates. Now a second open
> request for the same message is refused.
>
> I fixed it at two levels. The API checks for an existing pending request, but
> that check and the insert are two separate statements, so two simultaneous
> submissions could both pass. So there's also a partial unique index in the
> database — unique on email and requester, but only where the status is
> 'pending'. That makes the rule atomic, while still allowing a second attempt
> after a previous request was denied.
>
> Approving as the analyst updates the request, releases the underlying email, and
> writes both a review row and an audit row in a single transaction. If any part
> failed, the session rolls back and none of it is written.
>
> The larger fix came from asking what each action actually means. The API had no
> rule about which state an action could start from, so I could release an email
> that had never been quarantined — and it recorded that as a real analyst
> decision in the audit log. The valid transitions now live in one module the
> whole backend imports, the interface reads the same table so it never offers an
> action the server would refuse, and a test compares the two files so they cannot
> drift apart.
>
> On libraries: bcrypt for password hashing, PyJWT for tokens, and Pydantic for
> validation at the API boundary. That last one matters more than it sounds — my
> subject column is VARCHAR 500, and SQLite silently accepted longer values while
> PostgreSQL rejected them with an error the user saw as a 500. Validating the
> length at the boundary made both databases behave identically."

---

## Segment 5 — 3:10–4:00 · Testing, limitations and the repository

**On screen (3:10):** audit log, scrolled.
**On screen (3:24):** staff redirected away from `/audit`.
**On screen (3:34):** dashboard error state with the API blocked.

> "Every action is recorded here with the actor, the action, the entity, a
> readable detail and the IP address. The table is append-only at the application
> level — no route updates or deletes an audit row. I'm not claiming it's immutable
> storage, though: someone with direct database access could still change it.
>
> Access control is enforced server-side. As a staff member I'm redirected away
> from the audit page, and the API independently returns 403 — the route guard in
> the frontend is a convenience, not the control. Authorisation never trusts the
> role claim inside the token; it re-reads the role from the database on every
> request, so a tampered token grants nothing.
>
> And this is what happens when the backend can't be reached. It used to render
> 'No audit entries', which looks identical to a genuinely empty log, and the
> dashboard would sit on 'Loading' forever. Now there's an explicit message, a
> retry button, and a reference ID that matches the server log line.
>
> On testing: 170 backend tests with 90 per cent statement coverage, 92 frontend
> tests, and a 22-check script that drives a real running server end to end. The
> backend suite runs on SQLite and on PostgreSQL 16.6 and passes identically on
> both. All of it runs in GitHub Actions on three Python versions and against a
> real PostgreSQL container.
>
> Honest limitations: the detection is heuristic and will produce false positives
> and false negatives, which is exactly why a human reviews it. The SPF, DKIM and
> DMARC results are simulated, because my sample data has no real SMTP headers.
> The DistilBERT classifier is a documented placeholder — it is not built and not
> wired in. There's no live mail ingestion and no HTTPS in this local demo.
>
> The code, the setup instructions and this evidence are all in the repository,
> tagged v1.4-final. Thanks for watching."

**Recording notes**

- Record the real application, not slides — the brief requires it.
- Do not read code line by line; explain what it does and why.
- Nothing on screen exposes a password, key or private data. The demo accounts
  use the reserved `.local` domain and their passwords are documented test
  credentials.
- Confirm the exported file opens and has audible narration before submitting.
